packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a 5-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes but lower how trustworthy the advice is rated, especially when the default is refused, and framing of the default question itself (asking how much to leave safe vs. invest) shifts the outcome.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment on financial advice defaults.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests whether a financial default reads as helpful or manipulative in a European consumer context, and shows framing of the same default changes outcomes — both feed straight into the entry-design and level-anchoring decisions.
limitations: wealth-management risk allocation, not round-up savings specifically
advice-rating outcome is a perception proxy, not actual retention or amount saved
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer financial experiment on default framing and perceived manipulation, the closest direct evidence for the dark-pattern risk the brief flags.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged users often chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with six-month follow-up.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows that changing an enrolment default can move a headline enrolment metric while leaving the underlying financial behaviour essentially unchanged — the exact 'vanity enrolment' failure mode our support team predicts for round-up.
limitations: credit card repayment context, not savings
six-month horizon only, not 12 months
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed field experiment showing a nudge succeeding on enrolment optics but failing on the real outcome the brief cares about.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: In 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out effort cost together (friction complementarity); adding a lower preset option (15%) captured 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural model estimated on transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey; counterfactual simulations of alternative preset menus.
packets.why_it_matters: A direct, quantified test of how a menu of preset options anchors choices and what happens when you add or change presets — precisely the question of whether shipping 1x/2x/5x versus a blank field will anchor round-up levels.
limitations: tipping, not savings, so stakes and framing differ
single point-in-time choices, no persistence or withdrawal data
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative model of how preset menu design shapes which option consumers end up choosing, directly informing the level-anchoring decision.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrolment and of default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% (auto-enrollment) and 0.3% (auto-escalation), and only 40% of people escalate on the first date.
packets.methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job turnover, withdrawal on separation, and opt-out from auto-escalation; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative statement of our support team's objection: default-driven enrolment gains shrink dramatically once turnover, withdrawal and opt-out are accounted for over time.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated auto-escalation differs from a self-set multiplier
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably and durably raise saving, which the brief asked us to test.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default choice architecture does or does not produce lasting ('downstream') effects on consumer behaviour, identifying time course, prior preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
packets.methodology: Conceptual synthesis and research agenda; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a framework for exactly the persistence question the brief asks — what to measure and when to expect a default's effect to fade versus stick — useful for designing the 6-12 month follow-up analysis.
limitations: theoretical/conceptual, not new empirical effect sizes
general consumer behaviour, not financial products specifically
packets.relevance_reason: The review/synthesis giving a structured account of default persistence mechanisms the brief asks for.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Maps EU laws addressing dark patterns (including pre-selecting options by default) and develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable manipulation.
packets.methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis and taxonomy construction across EU law.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the regulatory framework for judging whether an opt-out enrolment design in an EU consumer banking app would read as a helpful default or a sanctionable dark pattern — directly shapes the legal risk assessment behind the entry-design decision.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not behavioural effect data
not specific to savings or fintech products
packets.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the brief's stated EU dark-pattern reputational risk for the entry-design decision.
packets.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
packets.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

packets.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but roughly 80% of employees initially accepted both the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years, largely offsetting participation gains against under-saving at the default level.
packets.methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms comparing pre/post automatic enrollment.
packets.why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that presets anchor people at the default level for years, which is the central risk of shipping a pre-selected round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a consumer app
classic study predating the current app/liquidity/regulatory context the brief says has since changed
packets.relevance_reason: The canonical anchoring-on-defaults result the newer literature argues with; included as the foundational reference point.
packets.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months versus roughly 50% at lower defaults typically studied, and many remaining defaulters had contribution rates far above what their income would predict.
packets.methodology: Empirical analysis of a firm's retirement plan with an unusually high 12% default, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the level of a preset default anchors people at a value they would not otherwise choose, which is exactly the round-up multiplier anchoring question, and shows anchoring can be stronger for lower-income users.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a liquid consumer savings product
no employer-trust-mechanism discussion
single-firm case study
packets.relevance_reason: Best available evidence that preset default levels anchor final contribution amounts and that this effect differs by income, directly informing the round-up multiplier default choice.
packets.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
packets.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making. Contributions: conceptualized paper (JB, DL, BM, JC), wrote paper (JB, JC), edited paper (DL), implemented empirical analysis (JB, RG), project leadership (JB, JC). The research reported herein was supported by the U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) through grant #10-M-98363-1-02 to the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) as part of the Retirement Research Consortium (RRC). The findings and conclusions expressed are solely those of the authors and do not represent the views of SSA, any agency of the Federal Government, the RRC, the authors’ universities, or NBER. The authors thank Joshua Rauh and two anonymous reviewers for their comments and thank Yeguang Chi and Richard Lombardo for excellent research assistance. The authors also acknowledge individual and collective financial support from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-AG021650 and T32-AG-000186) and the Pershing Square Fund for Research on the Foundations of Human Behavior.

packets.key_finding: A synthesis of household finance evidence covering savings, borrowing, payments, and asset allocation, and reviewing interventions including choice architecture, product design, and defaults used by firms and governments to shape financial behavior.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/book chapter summarizing empirical regularities and behavioral interventions in household finance; abstract-only for specific effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides the broad consumer-household-finance framing (rather than employer-retirement framing) for evaluating choice-architecture interventions like defaults and active choice, and is the kind of synthesis the brief wants to check the team's assumptions against before building.
limitations: broad review chapter, not a single quantified study
abstract does not isolate effect sizes for defaults specifically
covers many topics beyond savings-enrollment defaults, diluting direct applicability
packets.relevance_reason: The household-finance-specific review that can anchor the project's understanding of choice architecture in a consumer (not employer-plan) setting, satisfying the brief's need for a synthesis giving context rather than a single study's estimate.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: A randomized nudge (payment reminders) reduced credit-card late fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, concentrated among users with a history of overdraft use, so those users saw a 5% net increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment on a financial management platform in Brazil, credit card and checking account fee data.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer digital financial product can hurt a vulnerable subgroup even while helping most users on average — exactly the 'works on average by hurting those who did not need it' risk the brief asks about for round-up enrollment.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults specifically
Brazilian credit-card market, not EU regulatory context
abstract doesn't report enrollment/persistence over 6-12 months
packets.relevance_reason: A rigorous RCT in a genuine consumer fintech setting showing distributional harm from a nudge, directly contradicting the 'defaults/nudges always help' premise and matching the brief's call for heterogeneity evidence.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice,' a variant of active/forced choice that highlights losses from the non-preferred option, as a technique to motivate behavior change when opt-out defaults are infeasible or unethical.
alternates.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against standard defaults.
alternates.why_it_matters: Introduces the specific enhanced-active-choice technique — a forced-choice screen with loss framing on the non-round-up option — as a concrete design for the app's onboarding step, directly answering whether active choice can be structured to capture more of the default's benefit.
limitations: studies medication adherence, not financial products
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
review-style synthesis rather than a single definitive trial
alternates.relevance_reason: Names an explicit, transferable choice-architecture technique (loss-framed active choice) for exactly the entry-mechanism decision the brief is making, surviving the change from health to finance because the technique is generic to any binary opt-in/opt-out decision screen.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: Automatic (passive) contributions raise total wealth accumulation substantially, while active-choice subsidies mostly just shift assets between accounts, with each $1 of subsidy raising saving by only 1 cent; roughly 85% of individuals are passive savers unresponsive to subsidies.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel of 41 million observations across the Danish population, quasi-experimental variation in subsidy and automatic-contribution policies.
alternates.why_it_matters: The foundational large-scale evidence that passive defaults change actual saved amounts, not just nominal enrollment, and that most people are 'passive' — directly bears on whether defaults for the round-up feature would change real savings behavior versus just headline enrollment.
limitations: retirement/tax-advantaged accounts in a national pension system, not a liquid self-directed banking feature
no employer-as-intermediary caveat addressed
predates current EU fintech/dark-pattern regulatory context
alternates.relevance_reason: The classic large-N study distinguishing active vs passive savers and showing defaults move real savings amounts, which every later paper in this space argues with or extends.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, leaving only modest average savings increases though inequality in savings falls; a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost around $250.
alternates.methodology: Cross-plan and cross-country (US plans, UK panel) analysis plus a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question with a medium-run horizon, showing the enrolment lift decays well before it can be called durable.
limitations: employer retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
structural model estimates, not direct app-level data
alternates.relevance_reason: Best available evidence on how much a default's effect on participation and amount decays by medium-run horizons, directly bearing on the 6-12 month persistence question even though the setting is retirement plans.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)

alternates.key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default option causes substantial losses.
alternates.methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a government health insurance program; abstract-only for effect sizes.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows that default effects can persist even when the default is bad for the user, which bears directly on the risk that passively-enrolled round-up users could stay enrolled in a default that doesn't suit them rather than genuinely benefiting.
limitations: setting is Medicare drug plan enrollment for low-income beneficiaries, not a self-directed consumer banking app
no employer-analogy mechanism, but also no fintech mechanism
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
alternates.relevance_reason: Speaks to persistence and insensitivity of passive default effects, relevant to the distributional/manipulation risk question, though in a health-insurance rather than consumer-finance setting.
alternates.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
alternates.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

alternates.key_finding: An opt-in payroll-deducted short-term (liquid, withdrawable-anytime) savings account had very low take-up (under 0.7% of eligible employees) but strong persistence among adopters — 96% retained a balance and 87% received a contribution at month 12.
alternates.methodology: Field study of program rollout at five U.K. firms tracking account activity over 12 months.
alternates.why_it_matters: The closest empirical analogue to round-up savings (liquid, short-term, opt-in) available: shows opt-in can produce highly engaged, persistent savers but at a tiny enrolment rate, sharpening the trade-off the brief poses between entry design and engagement quality.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction context, not a self-directed banking app
no comparison arm with opt-out or active choice
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly on-topic for liquid, short-term consumer savings persistence, despite being employer-mediated rather than app-based.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.
